newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu asks that Bank of Israel bill be frozen.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu asks that Bank of Israel bill be frozen.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked to suspend deliberations on a private member's bill now in parliament creating a board of governors for the Bank of Israel, government sources said on Thursday.
Avraham Ravitz, chairman of the finance committee and one of the bill's two sponsors, confirmed the request but said he had no plans of suspending discussions.

The legislation would form a six-member board to determine monetary policy, which is currently at the sole discretion of the central bank's governor. The governor would chair the board and have two votes in the event of a split.
The bill, which enjoys broad support, is co-sponsored by Abraham Shohat, a former finance minister and a member of the opposition Labour party. Ravitz belongs to the government coalition.

The sources said Netanyahu's request came several days after he met Bank of Israel governor Jacob Frenkel and former Finance Minister Dan Meridor on June 16 to discuss foreign currency liberalisation and changes in the exchange rate mechanism.

The cabinet adopted the exchange rate reforms a day later, a decision that caused Meridor to resign charging the reforms had been implemented in a way that undermined his authority as finance minster.
Hours after the cabinet decision was taken, the Bank of Israel slashed interest rates 1.2 percentage points, a move that opened Frenkel to charges that the cut was politically motivated.
The Bank of Israel, however, denied there was any agreement between Netanyahu and Frenkel on the Bank of Israel legislation.

"The matter didn't come up at the talks," a spokesman said. "In February 1997, the ministerial legislative committee decided, in consultation with the finance minister...that all legislation in the matter would come at the government's initiative."

Frenkel has said he is not opposed to a board of governors but only on condition that the central bank's goals are legally re-defined to stress its role in controlling inflation in comparison with other policy goals.
Critics of Frenkel's restrictive monetary policy have been pressing for a board in the hope that a board would consider wider factors such as economic growth in setting interest rates.
Ravitz said the prime minister had asked him to freeze discussion on the bill because the government planned to introduce its own legislation.
